albums.blurb: Jim Hall was jazz's great understated guitarist, a favorite of Sonny Rollins and Bill Evans who valued space and tone over speed. Concierto, recorded in April 1975 at Van Gelder Studio for Creed Taylor's CTI label, sets him in an all-star sextet with Paul Desmond, Chet Baker, Roland Hanna, Ron Carter and Steve Gadd, with arrangements by Don Sebesky. Its centerpiece is a nineteen-minute reading of Rodrigo's Concierto de Aranjuez that filled the whole second side of the original LP.
albums.reception: AllMusic's Ken Dryden called it "arguably the greatest LP in CTI's history," and All About Jazz has described it as a high watermark for both the label and Hall.

albums.blurb: Swimming is the Pittsburgh rapper's fifth studio album and the last released in his lifetime, arriving on REMember/Warner in August 2018, five weeks before his death at 26. It completes his turn from party rap toward sung, live-band soul and funk, with Thundercat's bass threaded through its warmest moments, and it forms a deliberate pair with Circles, the companion album finished posthumously by producer Jon Brion in 2020.
albums.reception: It debuted at number three on the Billboard 200, earned a posthumous Grammy nomination for Best Rap Album at the 2019 ceremony, and was certified platinum by the RIAA in 2021.

albums.blurb: Betty Davis was a funk singer and songwriter — briefly married to Miles Davis, whose electric turn she helped catalyze — and one of the first Black women to write and produce her own records. They Say I'm Different, her second album, came out in 1974 on the Just Sunshine label and is her rawest, most snarling statement; radio largely refused to play her, and she left the industry by 1980. The album circulated as a collector's secret until Light in the Attic's 2007 remastered reissue brought it back into print.
albums.reception: It reached number 46 on Billboard's R&B albums chart, and The Wire later included it in its list "100 Records That Set the World on Fire (While No One Was Listening)."
